newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech crown surges but clouds on horizon-analysts.
newsitem.headline: Czech crown surges but clouds on horizon-analysts.

text.p: The Czech crown, which hit an all time high against its mark/dollar basket on Friday, is likely to remain strong in the medium term but a rising trade deficit will determine its fate thereafter, analysts said.

The Czech National Bank (CNB) fixed the crown on Friday at 27.274 to the dollar and 17.009 to the mark as the interbank market pushed the currency to a record of more than five percent above parity with its mark/dollar basket.
Foreign investors continued to pile into the crown, sending it more than two full percentage points higher against the basket since the start of this year.
The main new factor has been a 20 billion crown ($733 million) wave of Eurobonds this year, bought almost exclusivley by foreign investors, mainly from Germany, Luxembourg and Switzerland.
Late on Thursday the CNB unexpectedly announced 1997 money supply growth targets, at eight to 12 percent.
This allayed fears among crown investors of an imminent cut in interest rates to boost sagging economic growth, which slowed to 3.6 percent year-on-year in the third quarter of 1996.

"The Czech National Bank gave a clear signal that it wants to keep its monetary policy tight and...I don't think there is too much space for a decrease of interest rates this year if that target is met," said Pavel Sobisek of Zivnostneska Banka.

Interbank money market rates up to three months hover around 12.5 percent, creating an interest rate differential with major currencies which has formed the backbone of the crown's strength in recent months.
Inflation, stubbornly above nine percent for much of 1996 eased to 8.6 percent, year-on-year, in December.
Against this, the trade deficit has ballooned and the current account deficit is widely expected to hit eight percent of gross domestic product for 1996.
But state officials say that worries over a rising tide of imports should not be overstated and argue that a significant portion are investment goods, which will eventually help reinvigorate exports.

"I would like to believe what's declared by the Statistical Bureau -- that 75 percent of all imports have an investment character...If this is true this foreign trade balance should improve itself after some delay," said Emil Stava of Citibank.

"If this is not true...then it's basically bad luck and there'll be payback time after this delay. Then it would be really hot for the economy and some (crown) depreciation would eventually come," he added.

However, Stava said that the reckoning for the trade deficit would be unlikely to come in 1997, adding that the CNB had built up vast foreign exchange reserves -- $12.6 billion at the end of November -- which it could use to support the crown.
"There are lots of forex reserves which is quite costly for the National Bank to (manage). They would easily give a couple billion dollars to finance the foreign trade deficit," he said.
The Czech current account was in deficit by some $3.1 billion for the first nine months of 1996.

The Czech currency is fixed daily against the mid-point of a basket comprising 35 percent dollars and 65 percent marks. The crown can be fixed by the CNB at up to plus or minus 7.5 percent from the mid-point.
